key_claims: Subjective sleepiness maps linearly onto the signed distance between homeostatic pressure and the circadian-modulated sleep-onset threshold.
The distance can be decomposed into two mechanistically separable axes: intensity (time-averaged margin) and phase (circadian modulation of the threshold).
Slowed homeostatic accumulation accounts for the blunted sleepiness of older adults.
Pharmacological suppression of homeostatic pressure accounts for the dose-dependent alerting effect of caffeine.
Under forced-desynchrony, sleepiness tracks the circadian profile of the threshold while the intensity mapping remains unchanged.
limitations: The source is a preprint and may not have undergone peer review.
The framework is theoretical and may require further empirical validation.
The source does not provide specific quantitative details or effect sizes.
The source does not discuss potential limitations of the model.
what_not_to_say: The source does not claim that sleepiness causes drowsy-driving fatalities or medical errors.
The source does not claim that the model is the only or best predictor of sleepiness.
The source does not provide specific numbers or statistics.
The source does not claim that caffeine directly suppresses homeostatic pressure in all contexts.
